repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: At the beginning of the passage, the narrator assumes that the pale patch should be:
options: removed together with the damaged arm so the chair can be rebuilt.
dated through laboratory testing before any treatment is considered.
stained until it is no longer visible.
displayed separately as evidence unrelated to the rest of the chair.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: As used in the final paragraph, the word 'legible' most nearly means:
options: protected from every form of physical contact or later treatment.
returned as closely as possible to its original manufactured condition.
marked with enough information to establish a precise date and maker.
capable of being interpreted or understood.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Conservation requires judging which changes carry useful evidence and how honestly that evidence can be presented.
Conservation succeeds only when later alterations are removed so an object's original design can be shown without distraction.
Because repairs reveal an object's history more clearly than its original design, conservators should preserve every alteration they find.
Museums can interpret repaired furniture responsibly only when each alteration can be assigned to a known maker and exact date.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The drawer runner, shortened table leg, and covered upholstery in the third paragraph primarily serve to:
options: demonstrate that routine alterations usually result from flaws in an object's original design.
show several ways furniture records practical choices made after manufacture.
identify later repairs that conservators generally remove before an object is exhibited.
contrast the durability of walnut furniture with pieces made from less suitable materials.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Why does the author emphasize documenting a harmful repair before removing it?
options: Documentation can establish that a dangerous repair has become harmless enough to retain.
Written observations can provide museums with a complete substitute for the treated object.
Documentation can preserve evidence that the physical treatment will destroy.
Measurements can identify the person responsible for a repair even when no records survive.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The discussion of the repaired school desk implies that the same physical feature may be:
options: useful evidence of limited school budgets but irrelevant to questions about classroom history.
evidence of standardized manufacturing in both a classroom and a design exhibition.
too misleading to display unless the identity of the person who made it can be proven.
historically useful in one exhibition and distracting in another.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The final treatment of the walnut chair is best described as an attempt to:
options: balance visual coherence with the continued visibility of repair evidence.
make the patch visually dominant so visitors will notice it from across the room.
restore the chair to an original color that the conservators could document precisely.
give the patch a detailed historical identity despite the limits of the available evidence.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Which statement best explains the claim that evidence does not announce its own importance?
options: Physical marks become historically meaningful only after conservators remove the changes that obscure an object's original design.
The relevance assigned to a repair depends partly on the questions and context through which it is presented.
Repairs made by notable craftspeople deserve interpretation, whereas undocumented changes provide no dependable historical evidence.
Every surviving mark can support several equally convincing conclusions, so curators should avoid selecting among interpretations.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: By describing conservation as a less tidy responsibility, the narrator most nearly means that conservation:
options: succeeds only when treatment removes visible age while preserving a record of every decision made by an object's owners.
should retain every alteration as historical evidence even when later work threatens the object's physical stability.
requires choices among competing forms of value rather than a simple reversal of change.
can avoid uncertain interpretation when conservators document each mark before deciding whether it should remain visible.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: What is one disadvantage of a cool roost?
options: It requires bats to maintain a high metabolism throughout the resting period.
It exposes bats to dangerous water loss whenever afternoon temperatures rise.
It prevents bats from returning to familiar shelters when predator cues are absent.
A torpid bat may need more time to warm its muscles before flight.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Why did researchers rotate panels among boxes?
options: To separate temperature effects from preferences for particular locations.
To ensure that bats encountered the same exterior color at every location.
To compare changes in body mass among bats using different cliff locations.
To keep the owl recordings associated with one box throughout the experiment.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
options: Bats consistently conserve the most energy by selecting the coolest available shelter, regardless of immediate conditions.
Bats adjust roost choices as the benefits and costs of warmth change with conditions.
Bats respond primarily to the visible color of a shelter, while internal temperature has little influence on their choices.
Bats abandon familiar roosts after hearing predators and avoid returning to those locations during later seasons.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Why might warmer roosts be favored after owl recordings?
options: Warm exterior panels may make resting bats more difficult for returning owls to detect.
Heated walls may prevent later predator recordings from being heard inside the boxes.
Warm muscles may permit a faster departure if danger returns.
Higher roost temperatures may increase the number of insects available near the cliff.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The secretly heated boxes strengthen the thermal interpretation because they:
options: measured internal temperature without using the sensors installed in the other boxes.
tested the same panel treatments at a second canyon with different natural roosts.
kept bats inside after dawn long enough to compare their responses to later sounds.
changed internal warmth without changing the visible exterior cue.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Females carrying young likely favor warmth because:
options: young bats regulate temperature poorly and may grow more slowly when repeatedly cooled.
adult females lose the ability to enter torpor while they are caring for developing young.
warmer boxes prevent unrelated adult bats from occupying space needed by the offspring.
young bats must hear predator recordings before they can safely enter a resting state.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The hot-afternoon result demonstrates that:
options: temperature stops influencing roost choice once bats have responded to a predator cue.
a useful trait can become harmful beyond certain conditions.
dark exterior panels remain beneficial even when they raise the risk of water loss.
predator risk outweighs reproductive needs and weather in determining every shelter choice.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Which result most directly weakens the claim that bats merely avoided one cliff location?
options: Sensors showed that wall temperatures differed among boxes positioned on the same cliff face.
Some tagged bats remained in the cooler boxes until well after sunrise on mild mornings.
Preferences changed when thermal panels were rotated among locations.
Females carrying young favored warm boxes even when researchers played no predator sounds.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The passage treats apparent inconsistency in roost choice as evidence of:
options: random movement among shelters that cannot be connected to any measurable environmental pattern.
an inability to recognize familiar shelters after panels or heating treatments have been changed.
a permanent temperature preference established early in life and modified only by reproduction.
context-sensitive decisions among competing biological demands.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: According to Passage B, why does Rosa leave narrow gaps among boxes?
options: To keep each pantry's frozen products separate from the dry goods already assigned to it
To make heavily loaded carts easier for the arriving drivers to identify and inspect
To reserve space for labels that volunteers will attach after the vans reach the center
To provide places where volunteers can grip and shift boxes

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: In Passage A, Leah calls the paper grid her 'horizon' primarily because it helps her:
options: see future effects beyond the vessels' current positions.
predict when fog will lift by comparing visibility at different points along the pier.
preserve a permanent record of crossings that have already been completed.
combine the current-location information from all three computer screens in one place.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Which statement best expresses a central idea shared by both passages?
options: Public services function most effectively when workers prevent customers from learning that schedules or deliveries have changed.
Effective responses preserve the larger system instead of allowing one immediate problem to dominate it.
Paper plans give experienced workers more dependable information than digital systems during an operational disruption.
The fairest response to a public-service problem is usually the one that restores the original schedule as quickly as possible.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The bell in Passage A primarily represents:
options: the point at which Leah begins gathering the information needed to plan a crossing.
an outdated public signal that the narrator expects the computer system to replace.
a simple public signal produced after numerous constraints have been reconciled.
a warning that changing fog conditions have made the scheduled route unsafe to operate.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Why does Rosa avoid moving every frozen item immediately after the alarm?
options: She believes the temperature log shows that the freezer is still operating normally despite the alarm.
She learns that the neighborhood pantries lack enough available space to accept any frozen products.
She expects the arriving drivers to help the maintenance worker repair the freezer before loading begins.
A total evacuation could obstruct ordinary work and treat foods with different risks as identical.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: In Passage B, the narrator's view of Rosa's slow checking changes from seeing it as:
options: unnecessary delay to seeing it as preparation that preserved choices.
careful instruction for volunteers to seeing it as an attempt to avoid responsibility for the freezer.
efficient preparation of the morning loads to seeing it as the reason the aisles later became blocked.
a response to an expected freezer emergency to seeing it as a rule used only for ordinary deliveries.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Leah and Rosa are most similar in that each teaches the narrator primarily by:
options: explaining the reasoning behind every operational decision before an unexpected problem occurs.
using a disruption to reveal consequences that are not immediately visible.
allowing one urgent problem to interrupt routine operations so that it receives full attention.
asking the narrator to choose the final response independently and then evaluating that decision.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Leah's paper horizon and Rosa's handles made of air are most alike because each:
options: replaces digital equipment that cannot provide useful information during an emergency.
makes the reasoning behind operational decisions immediately visible to the public.
occupies space that initially appears unnecessary but protects later options.
prevents workers from having to revise an established plan when a disruption occurs.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Taken together, the passages redefine effective action as action that is:
options: fast enough to keep passengers and pantry volunteers from becoming aware of any inconvenience.
focused on the most visible part of a problem before considering less immediate consequences.
postponed until workers can develop a response that preserves the original outcome for everyone.
proportionate to the disruption and informed by its effects across the system.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: According to the third paragraph, the categories of concentration, exchange, and production describe:
options: three architectural zones that planners are expected to include in every modern library.
successive stages through which a traditional reading room develops into a production space.
activities that may occur in different places or at different times.
specialized services that are practical only in large urban branches with separate rooms.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: As used in the second paragraph, the word 'monumental' most nearly emphasizes that the reading tables were:
options: recently constructed as part of an ambitious municipal building program.
difficult for library employees to maintain as circulation increased.
reserved for officials who were permitted to request books from controlled stacks.
large and imposing.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Which statement best expresses the central claim of the passage?
options: Library change is best understood as the deliberate arrangement of several continuing and newer functions.
Libraries can meet contemporary needs only by replacing quiet reading areas with workshops and collaborative programs.
Small libraries can balance competing community needs only by distributing their services among adjoining public buildings.
Circulation remains the most dependable measure of success because newer activities ultimately increase the use of books.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The second paragraph primarily serves to:
options: argue that open shelving expanded only after municipal leaders reduced spending on formal education.
show that libraries had already been changing in response to multiple social and practical forces.
establish that early patrons preferred independent browsing and circulation aisles to formal reading tables.
demonstrate that architectural decisions have always determined which activities a public library can support.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The discussion of sewing machines and recording booths most strongly suggests that production spaces may receive disproportionate attention because they:
options: require equipment whose cost exceeds that of the library's quieter services and traditional collections.
serve mainly patrons who participate in projects instead of borrowing books or consulting reference materials.
produce changes that are easier to notice than changes in organization or collection use.
shift staff attention away from reference questions and toward the maintenance of unfamiliar equipment.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The rural library's use of headphones and reservable desks is presented primarily as:
options: a complete substitute for separating concentration and collaborative activity with permanent walls.
evidence that patrons seeking quiet study generally prefer municipal offices to the library itself.
a temporary arrangement intended to remain in place until the library can construct a workshop.
a flexible response that reduces, but does not eliminate, a scheduling limitation.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Which example most clearly demonstrates that the passage's three functions can support one another rather than merely compete?
options: An oral-history group searches newspapers before recording an interview.
A courthouse branch uses thick masonry walls to protect study rooms from programs in the central hall.
Staff add colored paths after newcomers have difficulty locating the quiet rooms along an outer corridor.
A branch located beside a university reserves more space for concentration than for exchange or production.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Why would the author most likely reject a rule requiring every library to devote equal space to the three functions?
options: The three categories describe only older libraries whose buildings were designed before open shelving became common.
Community needs, building constraints, and available alternatives change the useful balance among functions.
An equal allocation of space would prevent staff from recording circulation, reservations, and attendance as separate measures.
Production activities consistently require more space than concentration and exchange activities combined.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Taken as a whole, the passage treats tension among library functions as:
options: proof that each library must eventually choose one permanent institutional identity.
a temporary result of patrons being unfamiliar with production tools and collaborative programs.
a design problem that can be managed differently but not universally eliminated.
evidence that historical collections no longer serve the practical needs of modern patrons.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Desert annuals survive unpredictable rainfall primarily by having nearly all seeds germinate as soon as moisture reaches the soil.
Variation in germination timing distributes risk across uncertain conditions, though every timing strategy has costs.
Seeds buried deeper in a desert seed bank consistently remain viable longer because they avoid the dangers faced near the surface.
Researchers can identify the most successful germination strategy by comparing how many seedlings appear after a single storm.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The controls described in the second paragraph help a seed population avoid:
options: producing seeds with different coat thicknesses in response to conditions experienced by the same parent plant.
being distributed among soil depths and landscape locations that expose seeds to different environmental signals.
having every seed respond to a brief rain as though it guarantees a complete season.
depending on later moisture and suitable temperatures once an individual seed has begun the germination process.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The fourth paragraph primarily qualifies the comparison between a seed bank and distributing risk by explaining that:
options: dormant seeds avoid the immediate hazards faced by seedlings and therefore remain protected from environmental loss.
persistent seed banks are useful mainly in locations where rainfall arrives on a relatively dependable schedule.
seeds stored below ground eventually respond together once a favorable growing season releases their dormancy.
reducing the danger of one failed season exposes waiting seeds to other dangers.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Why does the passage indicate that researchers use both buried mesh packets and nearby plots?
options: The packets reveal below-ground seed outcomes while the plots reveal which schedules lead to mature plants.
The packets measure rainfall absorbed by buried seeds while the plots record changes in surface temperature.
The packets isolate rapidly germinating seeds while the plots contain only seeds that remain dormant for several seasons.
The two methods allow every seed to be followed throughout the study without disturbing its position or development.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Which finding would provide the strongest evidence that a persistent seed-bank strategy benefits a population over several years?
options: After one substantial shower, seedlings from rapid-germinating seeds emerge earlier and in greater numbers than seedlings from the seed bank.
Dormant seeds remain detectable at several soil depths after a growing season in which rainfall was dependable and plants reproduced.
Across alternating failed and favorable seasons, some stored seeds survive to germinate and replenish the bank after reproducing.
Seeds retrieved from mesh packets absorb water at approximately the same time as naturally buried seeds in nearby monitoring plots.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The final statement that many possibilities remain beneath the visible plants most nearly emphasizes that:
options: researchers cannot draw dependable conclusions about a seed population without removing and examining all of the surrounding soil.
every seed that remains dormant below ground will eventually become a visible plant during the next favorable growing season.
above-ground plants provide less useful evidence than dormant seeds regardless of the environmental conditions being studied.
the plants that emerge represent only some of the population's varied responses to uncertainty.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: According to Passage A, why does the narrator initially feel more like an exhibit label than a useful visitor?
options: Mara records the narrator's explanation instead of using the old tool immediately.
The apprentices disregard the narrator's repair instructions because they use newer methods in the renovated doorway.
The renovated theater has converted the former backstage work area into space for digital equipment and public displays.
Mara asks the narrator to describe the theater's old routines but not to remain when the building reopens.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Which statement best expresses a central idea shared by both passages?
options: Institutions preserve their traditions most successfully when they resist technologies that replace familiar tools and working methods.
Professional expertise becomes less credible when its development is connected to personal memories of earlier informal work.
Returning to former work can reveal that past experience remains useful in altered circumstances.
People understand the institutions where they once worked more clearly when they observe current changes without participating in them.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: In Passage A, the apprentices' arrival primarily changes the narrator's understanding of the visit by showing that:
options: Mara depends on the narrator because she lacks enough technical knowledge to supervise the apprentices' repair work.
the digital archive cannot preserve an accurate account of methods that were once demonstrated through physical tools.
the apprentices value traditional tools more highly than the equipment introduced during the theater's renovation.
practical knowledge can continue through use even when older customs disappear.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The references in Passage A to Mara's tablet, the illuminated floor panels, and Mr. Vale's brass keys primarily serve to:
options: contrast institutional methods while preparing the question of what can persist through change.
establish the narrator's concern that replacing familiar navigation methods has made the renovated theater less safe.
demonstrate that Mara plans to remove the remaining objects connected with Mr. Vale before reopening the building.
explain why the theater relies on apprentices who can learn new systems instead of workers experienced with older equipment.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: How does the planning meeting in Passage B affect the narrator's earlier desire to appear exclusively professional?
options: It confirms the narrator's fear that the board distrusts knowledge acquired through informal volunteer work.
It shows that practical experience and technical calculations can jointly support professional authority.
It leads the narrator to replace the proposed rainwater system with the less technical approach Mrs. Okafor prefers.
It persuades the narrator that earlier connections to the greenhouse should be omitted from future presentations.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: At first, both narrators respond to evidence connecting their past and present roles with:
options: pride that their former supervisors have preserved the particular working methods associated with each narrator's earlier role.
confidence that the institutions consider personal memory more valuable than the practical results of current work.
concern that the connection will limit how their present contribution is understood.
relief that returning to a familiar institution will allow someone else to assume responsibility for their present work.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Taken together, the endings of the passages most strongly support which conclusion about continuity?
options: Continuity can survive visible change when experience is adapted, transmitted, or incorporated into new work.
Continuity depends on retaining the physical setting and customary tools through which useful knowledge was originally acquired.
Continuity becomes meaningful only when an institution formally documents each former worker's individual contribution.
Continuity prevents people from developing professional identities that extend beyond their earliest institutional responsibilities.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: What is the passage's main idea?
options: Movable chairs consistently create conversations because flexible furniture removes the social boundaries between strangers.
Fixed benches should be replaced because their orientation prevents people sharing a public space from interacting comfortably.
Researchers can determine why visitors select particular seats by observing repeated patterns in their visible behavior.
Seating design shapes opportunities for behavior without fully determining why people act as they do.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Why was the stone wall useful to bus riders?
options: It offered a clear view of arriving buses and adjustable personal distance.
It remained warmer than the official benches during the hours when most riders waited.
It faced away from the plaza's busiest routes and protected riders from passing activity.
It contained built-in schedule displays that allowed riders to monitor delayed vehicles.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The three-day increase in conversations is presented mainly to:
options: demonstrate that the nearby musician, rather than the chairs or weather, caused strangers to converse.
illustrate why simultaneous changes make a causal conclusion uncertain.
show that unusually warm weather has no measurable influence on how visitors use public space.
establish that reopening the fountain ordinarily reduces social contact among people seated nearby.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: People moved face-to-face chairs more often because that arrangement likely:
options: made each chair more difficult to move without help from another visitor.
blocked the open views that solitary visitors used to monitor approaching buses.
demanded more direct attention than some solitary users wanted.
signaled that the chairs had been reserved for maintenance workers near the fountain.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: How does the passage relate flexibility to successful seating?
options: Flexible furniture eliminates the need to provide seating in locations designed for different activities.
Movable seats allow researchers to identify each visitor's private reason for choosing a particular arrangement.
Flexible furniture works best when planners establish one arrangement that visitors are discouraged from changing.
Flexibility lets users adjust the balance between connection and separation.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Which finding would best support the passage's conclusion without exceeding its limits?
options: A large majority of interviewed visitors report preferring the same bench for the same personal reason.
Different seating arrangements repeatedly attract different uses, though interviews reveal varied personal reasons.
A planner installs one new bench and concludes that its placement will reliably create friendships among strangers.
Movable chairs remain in their original positions throughout a study despite differences in visitors and schedules.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Why does the author call the study's limitation useful?
options: It establishes that public furniture has no consistent influence on visible behavior in shared spaces.
It permits researchers to stop gathering evidence once they have observed one strong seating pattern.
It redirects planners from controlling behavior toward supporting multiple choices.
It encourages planners to use the same varied furniture arrangement in every public plaza.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Which statement best expresses the passage's central claim?
options: The first reusable freight box transformed shipping once carriers recognized that reducing repeated cargo handling would save time.
Government standards committees contributed the decisive innovation, while engineers and carriers mainly implemented their rules.
Containerization became transformative through compatible design, operations, information, and institutional agreement.
Container shipping improved loading efficiency chiefly by eliminating port labor rather than moving work into new occupations and locations.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Why does the third paragraph emphasize a projecting latch and a weak corner?
options: To show that visible differences among containers were the main obstacle preventing companies from adopting shared designs
To establish that early transport boxes could not be repaired after repeated lifting weakened their structures
To explain why compatible containers also had to carry the same types and quantities of cargo
To illustrate how a small incompatibility can interrupt transfers across an otherwise connected system

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The fifth paragraph most strongly suggests that compatible containers became more valuable as adoption spread because:
options: each box could move through more transport modes and locations without being unpacked.
shared standards gradually required every carrier, port, and manufacturer to operate as one business organization.
redesigned ports could eliminate the cranes, schedules, and inland connections previously needed to transfer cargo.
physical compatibility allowed goods to cross organizational boundaries without shared records or identification systems.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Shared identification formats and standardized corner fittings are similar because both:
options: remove the need for independent carriers and ports by placing every transfer under one organization.
determine which types of cargo different companies may load into a compatible container.
allow separate participants to coordinate at a predictable interface.
solve problems that mattered before container routes expanded but became unnecessary after adoption.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Why does the passage resist identifying one person as the sole inventor of containerization?
options: Surviving records identify the organizations that adopted containers but provide no evidence about earlier freight experiments.
Reusable boxes became possible only after modern ports, railways, and highways had already been redesigned around them.
The metal box reduced cargo handling, but its visible design contributed less than the paperwork used to track it.
Demonstration, technical refinement, shared standards, and broad adoption made different contributions to the final system.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Which principle is most consistent with the passage's account of technological change?
options: A technically effective component may remain limited until surrounding systems can use it consistently.
The most visible object associated with an invention generally contains the innovation chiefly responsible for its success.
Standardization is most likely to succeed when participants have made no prior investments in competing equipment or procedures.
Once an interface becomes standardized, the economic and geographic consequences of adopting it largely disappear.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: As used in Passage B, the word 'anecdotal' most nearly describes information regarded as:
options: limited to temperature measurements collected remotely by satellites rather than at street level.
based on personal reports rather than systematic evidence.
certain to represent the experiences of every resident within the population being studied.
expressed in terms too technical for neighborhood residents to interpret or evaluate.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: In Passage A, the contrast between the empty playground and the busy bus stop primarily serves to:
options: demonstrate that measurements taken at playgrounds are less accurate than readings collected near public transportation.
argue that buses and waiting passengers create the most significant sources of heat within urban neighborhoods.
explain why fixed temperature sensors should be placed inside occupied buildings instead of along streets.
show that temperature alone does not determine the amount of human exposure.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The author of Passage A would most likely view the East Ward residents' route map as:
options: a useful source for identifying where additional measurements and activity data are needed.
evidence that calibrated instruments should be removed from heat studies in favor of residents' reports.
a complete measure of the indoor nighttime temperatures experienced by people along each marked route.
an unreliable source because residents included useful destinations located beyond the study's official boundary.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The discussion of an apartment remaining hot overnight in Passage A and the discussion of underrepresented night workers in Passage B both emphasize that:
options: night workers consistently experience higher temperatures than residents whose schedules keep them indoors after dark.
daytime neighborhood studies can miss important dimensions of heat exposure.
indoor nighttime temperatures can be measured accurately only through residents' memories and personal reports.
the first sudden heat of spring creates little risk for apartment residents compared with conditions later in summer.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Based on the final paragraph, when a thermal map and resident map disagree, planners should first:
options: combine the reported temperatures from both maps without first examining differences in their methods or purposes.
remove residents' reports so that personal memory does not influence the interpretation of calibrated measurements.
treat the discrepancy as a clue that scale, timing, use, or sampling requires investigation.
assume that whichever map identifies the warmer location has also identified the more important exposure.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Taken together, the passages suggest that making a heat study more precise requires:
options: collecting additional temperature readings while excluding accounts of daily movement that cannot be measured by instruments.
using official neighborhood boundaries to determine which routes, buildings, and residents should count as evidence.
selecting the mapping method that produces the most urgent-looking result and directing resources toward its hottest location.
matching reliable physical measurements to clearly defined questions about people, places, and times.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Which choice best explains why the limitations described in the two passages make the methods complementary rather than mutually exclusive?
options: Instrument surveys can test patterns beyond individual memory, while resident accounts can reveal use and access that instruments do not record.
The two methods are complementary because they contain the same sampling weaknesses and should therefore produce identical maps.
Resident workshops provide the calibration required by sensors, while instrument surveys ensure that every language group joins a workshop.
Each method becomes dependable only when planners discard evidence collected by the other method before comparing results.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: According to the passage, why did dealers sort cloth into grades?
options: To help mills estimate the fiber quality and processing needs of each load
To ensure that pale paper products were manufactured entirely from clean white linen rather than dyed cotton
To conceal seams, buttons, and other fasteners that could reduce the price a mill paid for a mixed bale
To discourage households from saving scraps whose small quantities made warehouse storage less efficient

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Wood pulp removed the hidden environmental and labor costs that had made the expanding rag trade difficult to sustain.
Rag dealers disappeared soon after the first successful wood-pulp experiments because textile fibers no longer served specialized uses.
The shift from rags to wood reorganized papermaking's supply, labor, and risks rather than simply substituting a better ingredient.
Sorting cloth contributed little to papermaking because mills had to inspect and process every scrap regardless of its assigned grade.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The theft and artificially dampened bundles are included primarily to show that:
options: adding water to cloth was a legitimate processing method used to produce stronger grades of paper.
government export restrictions quickly solved shortages by directing all available rags to domestic mills.
publishers encouraged collectors to acquire stolen textiles when ordinary household supplies became scarce.
high prices during scarcity encouraged attempts to capture value dishonestly.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Wood pulp reduced mills' dependence on rag markets mainly because wood:
options: could be produced as a planned industrial input rather than only recovered after another product's use.
could be converted into paper without the machinery and chemical treatments required to process textile fibers.
produced paper identical in strength and appearance to every grade previously manufactured from linen and cotton.
arrived at mills already classified because households sorted discarded wood according to its likely fiber yield.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The passage mentions later recycling businesses primarily to emphasize that:
options: rag warehouses generally became paper mills once dealers gained enough experience grading textile fibers.
classification skills from the rag trade remained relevant even as materials and markets changed.
the introduction of wood pulp made separating reusable materials by composition largely unnecessary.
textile collectors retained control over later recycling industries because they owned the established transport routes.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: The statement that the rag system transferred risk downward means that:
options: paper mills kept the safest and most profitable work while performing every hazardous sorting task inside their own facilities.
households protected collectors from changing market conditions by setting stable prices for the cloth they discarded.
less powerful participants bore low returns, unstable prices, and dangerous work within a profitable supply chain.
publishers accepted the financial losses caused by contaminated cloth rather than passing those costs to mills and dealers.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Why does the author reject the claim that wood pulp merely replaced an inferior ingredient?
options: The claim assumes that demand for printed material was declining when rag shortages actually resulted from increasing paper use.
The claim exaggerates the public recognition received by skilled sorters while ignoring the role of households and collectors.
The claim treats wood pulp as an unsuccessful experiment even though rag-based papers remained useful for specialized products.
It overlooks both the complex coordination achieved by the rag system and the new dependencies created by wood production.

repairs.subject: Reading
repairs.question: Recurring rhythmic figures function as:
options: signals that tell the audience when to stop clapping and leave the procession route.
substitutes for rehearsals that would otherwise teach performers how the larger form develops.
evidence that the ensemble's tempo and spacing remain unchanged throughout a performance.
checkpoints that reveal position in the larger form.

repairs.subject: Reading
